Magnetic sensors measure static or oscillating magnetic fields in units of fractions of a Tesla (T).
The magnetic field is traditionally denoted B and is a vector quantity.
The simplest magnetic sensors work by measuring the change in the local magnetic field of the earth caused by a substantial amount of ferro-magnetic material such as the steel housing of a grenade.
The earth's magnetic field is much stronger (about 5µT) than the one produced by the material but essentially constant on the scale of a kilometer.
One measures a difference signal between two magnetometers separated by a meter or so.
The magnetic field difference scales linearly with the distance (to first order).
One is effectively measuring the gradient of the magnetic field.
A changing magnetic field will induce oscillating currents in metallic objects which can be easily separated from the earth's magnetic field and can be measured.
The method used with handheld metal detectors is more sensitive to the depth of the material.
The data for the assignment has magnetic field measurements at different locations from a drone flying over a field following a scanning pattern.
